title-group.article-title: Bridging the Social Gap Through ‘Conscious Caring’: A Constructivist Grounded Theory of the Art of Caring for Older Adults With Dual Sensory Impairment

sec.title: Aim
sec.p: The aim of this study was to develop a conceptual understanding of the role of caring for older adults with combined vision and hearing impairment (DSI).

sec.title: Background
sec.p: Dual sensory impairment (DSI) impacts both listening and speechreading communication, function and social participation, meaning that older adults often require support and care to ‘age in place’ successfully. Family carers play a key role in supporting older adults with DSI to maintain social and physical health.

sec.title: Design/Methods
sec.p: This qualitative study uses Charmaz's constructivist grounded theory (GT) methodology. Data were collected between 2017 and 2019 and analysed using constructivist GT methods. Lengthy interviews with eight family carers of older adults living with DSI explored personal histories of DSI, relationships with families, social networks and health care professionals.

sec.title: Results
sec.p: This study demonstrates that caring in this context is predominantly social and ‘invisible’. To reduce the social effort of their family member with DSI and to maintain their own self‐identity, family carers adopted a ‘conscious caring’ approach. This is conceptualised as an approach to caring that supports family carers to access resources embedded in their social networks by bridging the gap between the dyad and their broader, more diverse social networks.

sec.title: Conclusion
sec.p: This study identifies that a reduction in both close and broader social networks limits personal, social and psychosocial resources and impacts the capacity of the dyad to renegotiate their roles, create and maintain their individual and shared social networks and successfully transition to living with DSI.

sec.title: Implications
sec.p: There is a gap in the literature regarding the impact of sensory impairments on complex communication, health and social care needs of older adults and the role that family carers play. Registered nurses require complex communication skills to support older persons with DSI during health and social care interactions. A better understanding of DSI itself, as well as understanding the key role family carers play in integrating care for their family member, is crucial to delivering person‐centred care.

sec.title: Impact
sec.p: This study addresses a growing social gerontological issue and identifies the role that family carers play in integrating health and social care for their family member with DSI. Better professional recognition of DSI and increased visibility of the challenges of living with DSI could help address barriers to effective communication between service providers, formal care support staff and those with DSI. Integrating family carers into care teams is critical to improving health and social care experiences for both caregiver and care receiver.

sec.title: No Patient or Public Involvement
sec.p: This study did not include patient or public involvement in its design, conduct, or reporting.

sec.title: Introduction and Background
sec.p: Often dismissed as a ‘normal’ part of ageing, dual sensory impairment (DSI), the combination of vision and hearing impairment, is projected to impact one in four older adults in Australia (Australian Institute of Health and Welfare [AIHW] 2021). DSI presents unique and complex challenges to both older adults and their families and is more than the sum of individual vision and hearing losses, compromising both listening and speechreading communication, function and social participation (Heine and Browning 2002, 2004; Centre for Welfare and Social Issues 2024). This means that one sense cannot compensate for the other, and older adults very often require support and care to ‘age in place’ successfully. Informal or family carers (hereafter carers) play a key role in supporting older adults with DSI to maintain social and physical health, well‐being and quality of life, yet are relatively invisible in policy, practice and research. This paper presents qualitative research exploring the role of carers in a DSI context. We introduce the concept of conscious caring, an approach to care designed to support carers in a DSI context and foster better integration with health and social care services. Previous publications (Dunsmore et al. 2020; Dunsmore et al. 2025) provide details of the broader study.

Sensory loss is a health and social care issue, underrecognised in policy, practice and health and social care service delivery (Lin et al. 2004; World Federation of the Deafblind 2018). Single and dual sensory impairments are poorly acknowledged, often normalised as part of ageing, and stigmatised (Pérez‐Garín et al. 2021); sensory losses are identified as priorities for the growing global ageing population, with prevalence projected to increase significantly (Schneider et al. 2012; World Health Organisation, [WHO] 2019, 2021; The World Federation of the Deafblind [WFDB] 2023). In Australia, DSI is a significant cause of non‐fatal disease burden (AIHW 2021), and the recent report of the Lancet Standing Commission (2024) identifies sensory loss (vision and hearing impairment) as a risk factor for dementia.

Older adults with DSI often rely on family support and assistance in navigating the healthcare system to support their preferences to ‘age in place’ and to facilitate social participation and engagement more broadly (Kendig et al. 2017). Aged care policies and legislation that prefer home care over residential care (e.g., Aged Care (Living Longer Living Better) Bill (Cth) 2013; Moore 2021) have seen the growth of informal caring for older Australians living with a range of health needs, identifying carers as an integral part of the Australian health and social care system. Caregiving is a dyadic process which involves complex social interactions and relational attributes. Carers can facilitate social engagement and opportunities for older adults with DSI, and their broader social networks may provide opportunities to link to health care and social support and resources (Dunsmore et al. 2020). However, the caregiving role in the DSI context is poorly acknowledged despite bridging a significant gap in communication at the client–health and social care interface. This is relevant to people with DSI who experience significant social, functional and cognitive effects (Lehane et al. 2017) which compromise health and social care interactions.

Dual sensory impairment (DSI) affects all age groups, with age an accepted defining factor in differentiating DSI population subgroups. Two distinct groups are acknowledged: (1) congenital and (2) acquired DSI after language has been developed and where the challenge is to maintain communication and social skills (Dammeyer 2014; Guthrie et al. 2016). The focus of this study is acquired DSI, after the age of 65 years, where sensory losses are generally attributed to age‐related conditions such as age‐related macular degeneration (ARMD), cataract, glaucoma and presbycusis (Guthrie et al. 2016; Heine and Browning 2015; Schneider et al. 2011). Variability in the severity of DSI exists across the lifespan, with combinations ranging from mild to complete sensory loss in either sense (Wittich et al. 2012). Recent global efforts to develop international consensus on a classification framework for DSI/deafblindness across the lifespan have improved capacity to define, research and develop strategies for those with DSI (Jaiswal et al. 2024; Paramasivam et al. 2023), including in older age. That said, policies and strategies in Australia for DSI in the older population remain poorly integrated and lack representation from older persons themselves.

While understudied, there is growing evidence of a range of complex health and social impacts among older adults with DSI (Simcock 2017; Jaiswal et al. 2023). These include a reduction in instrumental activities of daily living (IADL) and activities of daily living (ADL) (Brennan et al. 2006), which interrupts interaction with the physical and social environments, impacts day‐to‐day living and increases dependence on others, such as family, to help navigate their social and physical environment (Heine and Browning 2004). The Canadian Longitudinal Study on Ageing found that DSI in older adults is associated with loneliness, lower rates of social participation, reduced social network diversity and lower overall availability of social support (Mick et al. 2018). These social impacts threaten (Heine and Browning 2014) psychological well‐being, with functional impairment and loss of independence resulting in feelings of sadness, anxiety and social isolation (Bodsworth et al. 2011; Kiely et al. 2013; Simning et al. 2019).

Sensory loss is also associated with higher health care use and higher associated costs (Deardorff et al. 2019; Huddle et al. 2016; Reed et al. 2020). Evidence suggests that sensory loss in older adults is not prioritised during health care interactions, and that information is missed or poorly communicated (Dunsmore et al. 2024). Indeed, the conflation of DSI with ageing for older adults themselves means that the complexity of DSI is not communicated to their healthcare providers. Shukla et al.'s (2019) systematic review demonstrated an association between hearing loss and poor health care communication, while others highlight reduced access to health care (Sharts‐Hopko et al. 2010; Hajek and König 2020), increased need for accompaniment to health care visits (Reed et al. 2020), poor documentation of sensory losses in medical records and potential for adverse health outcomes (Dullard and Saunders 2016; Crews and Campbell 2004). In Assi et al.'s (2020) study of Medicare beneficiaries in the US, older adults with DSI report dissatisfaction with quality of care and health care communication. More recently, an Australian qualitative study of hospital experiences of those with multiple sensory impairments reported neglect, dehumanisation, disparate care and poor communication (Watharow 2024).

While health professionals can and should play a key role in ensuring that complex communication strategies are established in health and social care settings, they (i.e., health professionals) lack resources, support and education to assist with complex communication (Roets‐Merken et al. 2016; Dunsmore et al. 2024). Carers then become the default communication pathway, and are central to navigating complex systems, managing communication interactions and integrating care and social support for their family member.

sec.title: Methods and Methodology
sec.p:
The aim of this study was to develop a conceptual understanding of the carers' role in social inclusion for older adults with DSI. This qualitative research study presents findings from intensive interviews with eight (8) family carers for persons living with DSI. This study is part of a larger research project which explored the experiences of both older adults with DSI (n = 15) and their family carers (n = 8). This article reports on the family carers' experiences only. Lengthy interviews explored personal histories of DSI, relationships with families, friends, health care professionals and other carers, guided by the following research questions:
How does DSI affect the social experiences of older Australians and their family carers?
How do these experiences shape the way family carers identify, maintain and adapt their social networks and roles in a DSI context?

sec.title: Design and Theoretical Framework
sec.p: Charmaz's (2014) constructivist variant of Grounded Theory (GT) methodology was determined to be the most appropriate research approach. Constructivist GT is relevant to emerging areas of research, such as DSI, where there is a lack of theory development and research (Charmaz 2014) and where the focus is on meaning and experience (Burns et al. 2022). In addition, constructivist GT facilitates the identification of social processes involved in dynamic and negotiated elements of care in this context with a view to the development of relevant theoretical concepts. The philosophical underpinning of this approach aligns with symbolic interactionism (SI) (Carter and Fuller 2016). SI provides an approach to understanding social action and interaction, and health behaviours in a social environment (Carter and Fuller 2016; Joas and Knöbl 2009). This is highly relevant in a DSI context, where personal experiences of DSI are shaped by interactions with society and competing discourses of ageing and disability and aligns with the authors' social constructivist (interpretive) perspective of DSI as complex, socially situated and shaped by human action and interaction. Constructivism recognises subjectivity and the role of the researcher in the construction and interpretation of data. Family carers in this study shared personal experiences, aligning with the constructivist position of interaction and co‐construction of knowledge, positioning the researcher–participant relationship as central to theory construction to better understand the socio‐relational and caring processes unique to the DSI context (Carter and Little 2007; Charmaz 2008).

sec.title: Study Setting and Recruitment
sec.p: Recruitment for participants in the DSI context is complex, as DSI is relatively invisible, poorly acknowledged in health and social care settings and normalised as part of ageing. This study was conducted in metropolitan Sydney, NSW, Australia, where there is no defined national or state service specifically for older adults with DSI. Recruitment for potential participants was sought through Vision Australia (VA) sites, as previous work indicated that many older Australians accessing services for VI also reported hearing loss, wore hearing aids, or had independently sought help from an audiologist prior to their VA appointment (Schneider et al. 2014). This made VA sites an obvious choice for recruitment because they offered information‐rich cases directly aligned with the study focus, making it a theoretically appropriate starting point for GT sampling. Author 1's presence at VA sites meant that face‐to‐face contact with potential participants was established early to communicate and explain study information.

sec.title: Sampling in Constructivist GT
sec.p: GT methodology has specific sampling techniques that support the advancement of theoretical development based on the emergence of categories; this occurs in parallel to data analysis and conceptual development (Birks and Mills 2015). Morse (2007) identifies specific transitions in sampling, including convenience, purposeful and theoretical sampling. In this study, convenience sampling identified potential participants who met eligibility criteria from the VA initially, and we were able to transition to purposeful sampling after the first three interviews and refine the direction of the interviews based on codes that emerged from these early interviews. As the study evolved and emerging categories were refined, theoretical sampling then sought specific participant characteristics to confirm or refine categories. For example, through a constant comparative approach, it became clear that DSI was a ‘shared experience’, that family carers were fundamental to shaping and negotiating the social experiences of their family member with DSI (see Figure 1).

sec.title: Data collection
sec.p: Intensive interviews are the most common form of data collection in constructivist GT and provide a flexible approach to gathering ‘rich’ data (Charmaz 2014; Conlon et al. 2015). A series of guided questions (known as sensitising concepts) was used to stimulate discussion. These guided questions were drawn from an international social capital framework (Siegler 2014), which provided structure and concepts broadly relevant to exploring the social experiences of carers. These concepts (see Appendix 1) were merged with key opening questions and seen as ‘points of departure’ to guide exploration rather than define emerging concepts (Charmaz 2014, 30). For example, the social capital concept of ‘trust, reciprocity and participation’ framed questions on professional trust (e.g., GP) and community support. Each semi‐structured interview lasted approximately 90 min, and all interviews were recorded and transcribed verbatim with participant permission.

sec.title: Data management, transcription and storage
sec.p: Transcripts were reviewed in conjunction with the recording to check for errors and missing data. Transcription was externally sourced by a professional transcription service, and hard copies of transcripts were scanned and stored in a password‐protected University of Sydney‐owned computer.

sec.title: Data Analysis
sec.p: Data analysis was framed by constructivist GT methods described by Charmaz (2014). Specific ‘tools’ inherent within the constructivist approach, such as constant comparative analysis, memo‐writing and theoretical coding and category development, were employed throughout the analytic process. Theoretical coding in GT is the first stage in the analytic process leading to theory development (Charmaz 2014; Tie et al. 2019). We followed constructivist GT guidelines and began systematic preliminary coding from the first interview. Codes were grouped and compared, a process described by Charmaz as ‘focused coding’ (Charmaz 2014, 140). This process provided early direction for future interview questions and helped foster theoretical sensitivity to emerging data.

Coding and category development were supported by reflective memo writing and provided a central link between data and emerging theory. These were drafted following interviews (named as ‘first thoughts’) and later as a way of describing codes and emerging detail. Memos form an audit trail of the deliberations and developing theories of the researcher, demonstrating rigour in the research process (Hoare et al. 2012).

Theoretical saturation is commonly used to justify sample size in qualitative research. GT saturation refers to the ability of the sample to deliver rich detail that supports theory, rather than to the number of participants interviewed (Hennink et al. 2019). A priori sample sizes do not readily align with the constructivist perspective of emergence and theoretical sampling, and there is a good argument to analyse small sample sizes (Crouch and McKenzie 2006). In this study, when new data did not generate new theoretical ideas or new properties of theoretical categories, we were confident that theoretical saturation had been achieved, and data collection was therefore concluded (Charmaz 2014).

sec.title: Ethical Considerations
sec.p: Confidentiality of participants' data was maintained through the use of pseudonyms applied to all participant transcripts to de‐identify data. Ethical approval for the project was granted through the Human Research Ethics Committee (HREC) at The University of Sydney, NSW, Australia (HREC 2014/897). Ethical approval for site recruitment was obtained in writing through Vision Australia, NSW, and verbally at a vision‐impaired community support group meeting.

sec.title: Rigour
sec.p: Carter and Little (2007) advocate for strong theoretical positioning as fundamental to ensuring rigour throughout. Charmaz (2014); Charmaz and Thornberg (2021) has identified constructivist‐specific evaluation criteria to establish theoretical rigour, and these four criteria were used in this study to determine theoretical rigour: (1) usefulness or knowledge development—this study addresses the lack of detailed qualitative research on lived experience in DSI and contributes to the development of potential new policy and practice applications; (2) credibility is underpinned by grounding data in participants' experiences and ‘having sufficient relevant data for asking incisive questions about the data, making systematic comparisons, and developing a thorough analysis’ (Charmaz and Thornberg 2021: 315). This was achieved through sustained contact with participants over long periods of time through VA clinic presence and support group attendance, as well as the use of theoretical sampling to enable critical analysis and emergence of thick, rich description; (3) originality—this study takes a unique approach to identifying DSI as a shared dyadic experience with significant social impacts on both; and (4) resonance—formal member checking and sustained contact with family carers over time indicated concurrence with the main findings.

sec.title: Findings
sec.p: This section explores two major themes related to the social experiences of caregiving in a DSI context. Theme 1 ‘reimagining caring in a DSI context’ includes three sub‐themes: (1) negotiating a new role, (2) active and passive transitions and (3) minimising DSI (see Figure 1). Theme 2, ‘the art of caring’, explores the concept of ‘conscious caring’, which includes (1) empathic understanding, (2) social facilitation and protection, (3) social engagement and (4) enabling a safe space.

sec.title: Theme 1: Reimagining Caring in a DSI Context
sec.p: This theme describes the ways family carers sought to understand their role, maintain their identity and independence within their caring relationship and the barriers that limited their access to informal and formal support (health and social care) networks (Figure 2).

caption.p: Reimaging caring in a DSI context.

sec.title: Negotiating a New Caring Role
sec.p:
Family carers lacked a critical understanding of the social aspects of their caring role; key duties, such as social facilitation and being the ‘eyes and ears’, were not necessarily aligned with their understanding or expectations of caring. While they understood the safety and physical aspects of their role—‘she might hurt herself or do something while I'm not here’ (Ted), navigating the communication and social needs of their family member with DSI was a more subtle and complex task, exhausting and potentially minimising access to the web of support available to them as carers. Many family carers were ageing (see Table 1) with their own health issues impacting their capacity to fully engage, recognise and adapt to their new caring role. In this study, caring involved increased social effort, which exceeded normal relational expectations and responsibilities. In addition, significant interpersonal tension existed, reinforced by the limited recognition of family carers by their family member with DSI, and adding to relational tension:
I, in my heart, am doing this for her and I get this look, and it gets me angry. I'd hate to be out enjoying myself and find I've come back and find her lying on the floor. (Ted)

For some carers, the progressive nature of DSI and the anticipation of increasing responsibilities were overwhelming:
So [I] didn't know whether I would be able to cope. Thinking that, you know, it's going to change our whole lifestyle. (Gail)

These responsibilities often resulted in missed opportunities for time out on their own—‘put it this way, I wouldn't go away for a day or two’ (Mary)—and all carers, particularly daughters, had some difficulty establishing personal boundaries. Struggling with time management issues and few opportunities to plan effectively led to a sense of ‘feeling stuck’, and while there was recognition of the need for self‐care, this was challenging to implement. Sarah described her experiences in the context of growing responsibilities and stressful miscommunication:
I really had this feeling like I've got to get out of here. … I felt like I was under a lot of stress. (Sarah)

More broadly, poor public recognition of DSI meant that adapting to their caring role was exacerbated by a lack of available or appropriate external support that could potentially facilitate ‘self‐care’. Shared care and support acceptable to their parent or spouse with DSI was limited, and there was often a reluctance by their family member with DSI to ‘share’ care with anyone outside of family, meaning negotiations to integrate formal systems of caring could be complex. Eve's (May's daughter) attempts to seek support and create opportunities to manage her part‐time work commitments were met with barriers. Formal (government‐funded) service models of care generally provide intermittent task‐orientated care, such as cleaning or personal care, rather than person‐centred care. For May, this meant her communication and social difficulties were not considered central to her care needs. The introduction of formal (paid) support created tension, as this was often resisted by the person with DSI:
Mum could be very argumentative about things, getting very stressed and you know constantly [saying]: ‘You know I just can't bear this next week’. Too busy. ‘I just want everybody to leave me alone, I don't want anyone coming in, I'm much happier when there's nobody calling’. … then there would be the lead‐up, the actual week and then the recovery. I felt so tired, you know, this has really taken it out of me. (Eve, daughter of May)

sec.title: Transitioning to a Caring Role
sec.p: Family carers adopted different ways of transitioning to the carer role, described in this study as active or passive. Active and passive transitions represented a balancing act, with descriptions of this process suggesting elements co‐existed (see Figure 3). Active transition described intuitive and often deliberate ways of caring, conceptualised in this study as conscious caring, while passive transitions were often ad hoc. The data suggest that the strength of carers' external networks was important in this transition process.

As noted in Table 1, three of the eight carers in this study were daughters, with an age range of 52–72 years. While these carers generally experienced good health, they were also busy with other life commitments. Daughter carers described more intuitive responses than older spousal carers to the more frustrating aspects of caring, recognising their needs as important: ‘it's two people to look after, not one’ (Eve). However, role ambiguity was pervasive—‘I'm the carer, you know more than the daughter’—and required skill and insight to manage effectively.
I really have to think sometimes ‘don't be frustrated about it’. Because it doesn't make any difference. The only person that suffers from that is me. (Eve, daughter of May)

Although Sarah recognised that reserving time for herself was important for her own health and well‐being, she still experienced guilt:
I'm going to be more careful to reserve a certain part of the day, which I can predict, for my mother—I'm going to be out from this time to this time…. I should do it because otherwise I get too depleted if I don't let myself have this certain time. I even feel guilty if I picked up something to read. (Sarah, daughter of Ina)

These participants actively sought external support and demonstrated insight into the social and communication aspects of DSI and the complex role they performed; however, they also recognised that maintaining their own identity within this caregiving relationship was important.

Carers described a combination of both active and passive transitioning. For some spousal carers, the ability to adopt different ways of caring that might have supported their own needs was more limited, and often ‘passive’. As spouses, there was an established and longstanding partnership with a shared identity, networks and familial obligations. They experienced shrinking networks and complex health needs of their own, which meant less flexibility in accessing external networks and fewer opportunities to prioritise their own needs. For Ted, there was difficulty adapting, compounded by poor interpersonal communication and a lack of acknowledgement of his role by his wife and family. Critically, the lack of external health and social support intensified his isolation. As he stated:
There's going to be a clash somewhere when you're altogether, all the time. No matter what your motives are, whether you really want to or whether you don't, there's going to be a clash. I just think it's—both of you being able to accept each other and try and help each other to do that. (Ted)

Paul's experience differed—his role as carer was more easily defined as Betty had multiple other health issues, meaning that Paul's caring role was more traditionally task orientated—'I have to dress her and everything … I dry her feet, put Vicks VapoRub on her big toes’—with less emphasis on Betty's severe DSI. They had planned ahead, moving to smaller accommodation in anticipation of Betty's increasing osteoarthritis and mobility issues, and their extensive family network was a presence in their life. It was clear that while DSI limited Betty's social engagement, Paul effectively ‘bridged the conversation gap’—often answering on Betty's behalf. He understood his caring role as ‘a partnership … you can't have one without the other’ and felt that it was ‘his turn to show how much I appreciated it’. Throughout the interview, there was a sense that Betty enjoyed her more passive social participation, only becoming animated when the discussion focused on shared past experiences. Paul's transition to carer was, in effect, enabled by Betty's acceptance of her role as care recipient.

sec.title: Minimising DSI
sec.p:
The intangible social aspects of caring, coupled with poor understanding of DSI, impact at this microsocial level, with carers, health providers and those with DSI all, unsurprisingly, minimising the impacts of DSI. Carers' assumptions of DSI as a normal part of ageing were reinforced at multiple levels: by their own understanding or lack thereof, and poor access to specific support and education. The limited recognition of DSI in public and primary care settings reinforced this misconception and further obfuscated DSI as a potential source of negative health and social impacts. Minimisation controlled the dialogue on DSI, particularly during health care interactions, despite DSI's clear impact on communication and engagement. Sarah drew attention to this in her interview:
“There's another thing too about the GP, the sort of mentality ‘Well what do you expect? You're 95’. Hearing and vision loss in old age is not seen as a disability, it's seen as something else.” (Sarah)

Minimisation meant that many family carers experienced significant social burden without necessarily understanding why or positioning themselves to seek further support. Family carers needed the space and time to process what was going on, to understand the nature of their caring role and to plan ahead. As noted earlier, the systemic barriers (e.g., poor recognition and acknowledgement of DSI) contributed to these complex social outcomes and delayed provision of appropriate support (if available) for both family carers and their family member with DSI. These factors significantly impacted their own capacity (in a context of ageing and comorbidities of their own) to navigate changed circumstances and transition to their new caring role.

sec.title: Theme 2: The Art of Caring—Conscious Caring
sec.p: The art of caring is conceptualised as ‘conscious caring’, which recognises the complex social aspects of caring in a DSI context. Conscious caring (Figure 4, Dunsmore 2022) describes family carers' social experiences, which many participants felt were poorly understood at the microsocial level and relatively ‘lost’ in a structural framework that normalises the disabling impact of DSI. Conscious caring reflects a process of social change that illustrates the impact of DSI on the complex interdependence of family carer and care receiver.

caption.p: Conscious caring—a complex process of social adaptation to the unique experiences of caring for an individual with DSI (Dunsmore 2022).

sec.p:
Family carers play a crucial role in facilitating social interaction for their family member with DSI, and the perceived effort involved relies on the carer's empathic understanding and sense of agency within the relationship. Gail's narrative highlighted how empathy guided her actions within different contexts. She described a need to let go of their existing, often traditional, roles and to focus more on their actual capabilities to enable a safe space that also created practical opportunities for Clive to retain some independence. She understood when to intervene, particularly during negative social interactions:
Clive can hold his own; it's just that sometimes in a group situation, people tend to have a conversation … you know they have eye contact, and they don't use names; you actually just have eye contact. So, if I'm speaking to you [Author 1], I don't necessarily have to use your name, because you know I'm speaking to you. But Clive doesn't; he sits there, and someone's tried to say something to him, and then when they don't get a response, they turn away. (Gail)

Gail adapted her social responses to suit the occasion. She understood that Clive would potentially find most social encounters difficult without her presence. Casual social experiences reinforced how DSI was invisible to others, reinforcing the need for social facilitation and protection in social encounters:
If I am with Clive, he doesn't take his cane. So, we can be at Bunnings or something, and the attendant is talking to Clive about screws or something, and I'm standing there thinking, ‘Oh God! He can't see’. You have to actually tell them, and they're very kind. You have to remind people [of his hearing] you know, ‘Speak up, he can't hear you’. (Gail)

In other social circumstances, responses were more tailored. Gail experienced this social rejection as a shared experience with potential consequences of isolation for both. She noticed that on meeting new people, ‘as soon as they've been introduced, they kind of move away, it's like someone who's got leprosy or something’ (Gail).

For some participants, caring was a somewhat passive role, which involved a task‐orientated approach but did not necessarily engender or facilitate social interactions, create opportunities, or foster independence for their family member with DSI. Maggie's ability to care effectively was influenced by Stuart's mood: ‘I don't like him upset and if he can't do things, then he gets upset’, prompting her increasing support: ‘I even cut his food up, I don't mind’ (Maggie). This differed from Gail's experience, whose understanding of DSI promoted sustainable links to their individual and shared social networks and a degree of independence for both. There was an art to balancing support for individual needs with overprotection and of encouragement versus forcing social participation; these internal negotiations existed across all social networks, including during health care interactions:
He is not stupid; he's deaf. He's not stupid, and I have become terribly protective of him, you know. Particularly when he was in hospital, I was very protective of him, probably more so than I should have been. (Mary)

Others described the effort taken to enable social participation with their family member, and the lengths they went to do this. Encouragement to ‘have a conversation, go to the local shops to pick the pint of milk up, go around instead of ringing her neighbour to ask something’ (Eve) was often met by reluctance from their partner or parent with DSI. Micro tactics—such as ‘slowing … speech down … try and speak in the lower ranges so it's clearer, but pretty much I repeat everything’ (Sarah)—were used to encourage conversation. Nevertheless, there was broad recognition of the gradual loss of cognitive processing ability—'losing the ability to listen’ (Sarah). The motivation to encourage interaction was often driven by concerns about cognitive decline and potentially losing the art of conversation, which is integral to everyday social interactions.

Some family carers actively facilitated engagement in shared social networks, often to the exclusion of their own. Maintaining independent networks, while important, was difficult. For example, Gail travelled extensively and independently of Clive, describing this as an important part of her identity. She reflected on her agency to do this, despite Clive's significant disability, on the way this shaped her attitude to Clive's disability and the benefits her agency had on their relationship:
Clive's been very thoughtful of me wanting to travel and he was quite happy to stay home here, and I had a friend pop in, or his daughter would come from Brisbane, stay a week or so. But he was still happy for me to go. And then I decided, ‘No, he's 92, it's really getting to the stage where I really should be home all the time’. So, since I made that decision myself, I think I'm a lot more tolerant of the problem. (Gail)

Recognising and accepting their family member's disability in their own time was important for participants' transition to the caring role. Protecting their own well‐being was a two‐way process, enabled by the interactions between family carer and care recipient, and strengthened by their external networks.

In the absence of strong family support, family carers looked to other external networks to help them in their caring role. Support groups, such as vision‐impaired community groups in Sydney, while not specific to DSI, provided some opportunity for carers to meet others in a similar situation. For instance, it provided incidental social opportunities and limited time out for Maggie, although not necessarily conferring the same benefits to her husband: ‘Yeah, it's good for me but not for Stuart’ (Maggie). These opportunities offered avenues for support for Maggie—'I have some friends there who give a big hug and, “How are you?”’ (Maggie)—but did not necessarily offer resources or information relevant to DSI. Sourcing appropriate and specific formal support was difficult, with government‐funded community service provision for older persons acknowledged as low‐paid and insecure, with little specific complex communication training related to DSI. Both Eve and May described communication difficulties with formal carers and a lack of choice and consistency in carer provision from aged care services, which meant that both were reluctant to engage in this form of external care:
It needs to be someone who speaks reasonably good English, and there aren't any … it's got to be people who are able to put the time and effort into building that rapport and all that kind of thing. (Eve)

Both Eve and May referred to the importance of external carers having good communication skills to facilitate a relationship with the person with DSI and, importantly, provide appropriate carer respite.

The skills for conscious caring were not wholly dependent on family carers' intuition but were a reciprocal interaction shaped by relationship strength and access to other means of socialising that were acceptable to both. Conscious caring is a dynamic process that benefits from external support for family carers to actualise their caring capacity and increase their ability to ‘live with’ DSI.

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: The aim of this study was to understand the social meaning and experiences of DSI from the perspective of family carers/family members, and to understand the unique aspects of caring for an older person with combined vision and hearing loss (DSI). The findings identify that the carers' role in a DSI context is poorly recognised by others, including by health and social care professionals. Importantly, the specific aspects of caring, such as complex communication, facilitating social interaction and social protection, are demanding, and despite carers' significant efforts to facilitate social opportunities for both their family member with DSI and themselves, the lack of visibility of DSI restricts their understanding of why caring in this context is so demanding. This study identifies the strategies and actions taken by carers to reimagine their caring role and suggests ‘conscious caring’ as a theoretical explanatory concept encapsulating the processes involved and inherent meanings within caregiving in a DSI context.

Our findings support the extant literature on intersectionality, specifically ageing into a disability, particularly in relation to the lack of visibility and support extended to older adults with DSI, and how these impact carers and families more broadly. The effects of combined vision and hearing loss [as DSI] are less well understood than single sensory loss (vision and hearing), with DSI lacking visibility in contemporary ageing and disability discourses. Ageing stereotypes, most often ‘negative’, were internalised, normalised and reproduced by participants in this study, shaping the way carers recognised and transitioned to their caring role and influencing their capacity to maintain their social networks and social identity with family and friends. Further, the diagnosis of DSI is a vexed issue in Australia and elsewhere (Simcock and Wittich 2019). Consistent with other studies (such as Burton et al. 2015), the lack of diagnostic clarity of DSI described by carers in this study shaped their social and health care interactions, and those of their family members. The fragmentation of services and lack of recognition of the multiplicative effects of DSI at a primary care level meant that DSI was minimised and conflated with ageing, and caregiving roles were ignored. This absence of an acknowledged identity can create distress (Montgomery and Kosloski 2012). Callero (1985) describes ‘role‐identities’ as ‘shared, socially recognized, and defined by action’ (p. 204), suggesting that caregiving is inherently social and interactional. When the disability or care needs are ‘invisible’, such as DSI, significant interpersonal strain and caregiver burden may develop, particularly in the absence of support from wider social networks and health professionals (Magliano et al. 2005).

We identified several barriers to transitioning to a caring role: first, the aforementioned lack of diagnostic clarity, misunderstanding of DSI itself and no recognised carer role identity meant transitions for carers were not necessarily constructive. Informal caring in a DSI context was relatively invisible beyond the caring dyad and poorly acknowledged within the dyad. Second, the caring role itself conflicted with participants' expectations of ‘traditional’ caring work. Understanding exactly what legitimised ‘care’ was shaped by stereotypes, ageism and the experiences of others, meaning that task‐orientated care was more broadly accepted and understood as a ‘caregiving identity’ (Monin et al. 2017). The dominant focus in a DSI context was, however, social and relational—‘being the eyes and ears’ in social contexts, and carers had little clarity on what was expected of them. This situation could exert strain on close relationships and play a key role in older couples' ability to accept, adjust to and cope with relationship changes caused by ill health or disability, such as DSI (Horowitz et al. 2004; Yorgason et al. 2006). Although Vassilev et al. (2011) suggest that illness knowledge is contextualised through social networks, the absence of DSI‐specific knowledge and restriction of social networks meant that carers in this study had little access to support or information, either professional or ‘lay’, to gain such knowledge.

Stress and coping are central themes in caregiving experiences and carer burden (Pearlin et al. 1990); however, it is the social relational care aspects of DSI that position the care dyad as critical in reducing care burden and ‘bridging communication and social gaps’. Shared identity theory (Lang and Fowers 2019) focuses on the dyad and the relationship rather than the individual caregiver and care burden, providing a perspective on the importance of shared goals and understanding at a dyadic level. However, in this study, while social relational impacts were evident, there was a disconnect within the dyad in recognising their new roles and identities as DSI progressed; the process of identity changes was not necessarily linear, was poorly communicated and involved multiple small modifications within and external to the dyad.

A conscious, caring approach recognises the unique aspects of caregiving in a DSI context from the carers' perspective. This approach, derived from lived experience narratives of carers in this study, builds on the premise of shared identity theory, that understanding and supporting the dyadic relationship is critical to supporting the dyad through the progressive, predominantly social impacts of DSI on families and family carers. The conscious caring approach identifies four key aspects of caring (see page 21, Figure 3) designed to facilitate social adaptation to the unique experiences of caring in a DSI context. Carers specifically describe increasing social isolation and reduced capacity to take ‘time out’, which limits capacity to strengthen and maintain both their relationship and the social networks that would potentially be of benefit to them and their family member. Other than the direct health benefits of improving mood and reducing cognitive decline (Berkman et al. 2000), social networks can facilitate access to health knowledge and impact health‐related quality of life (Rhee et al. 2021). A ‘conscious caring’ approach understands that facilitating access to broader networks, that is, social care networks beyond the dyad, has the capacity to reduce carer burden and positively impact the dyad.

The carers' experience of increasingly limited social networks and their own lack of understanding of DSI interrupts the continuum of care in the DSI context and limits capacity to create and maintain social and health networks (both formal and informal) that may benefit the dyad. In this study, the need for empathy, a critically important factor for effective conscious caring, is highlighted (e.g., in Gail's narrative) because empathy enables carers to recognise perceptions and emotions of those living with DSI, but the absence of external support left carers isolated to negotiate their new role without support. Unsurprisingly, extant literature suggests an absence of person‐ and family‐centred models of care designed to support carers in the DSI context. Quigley et al.'s (2022) qualitative study found that carer burden increased when interacting with complex and multiple systems (health, social and aged care systems). DSI presents challenges for health care interactions and health literacy, compounded by the complexity of the Australian healthcare system itself, which lacks support provision, rehabilitation options and care relevant for those with DSI. Mastering these complex systems is dependent on carer capacity, health system literacy and successful advocacy for their family member (Funk et al. 2019). In this study, family carers were clearly key to communication, creating a third‐party presence that shifted the power dynamics during health care interactions, limiting shared decision making and potentially introducing conflict (Barone et al. 1999). The more passive role of participants with DSI during health care interactions enabled a doctor–carer relationship to dominate, leaving carers uncomfortable and unable to accurately discuss key issues relevant to their partner or parent. Developing a ‘conscious caring’ environment to support carers in their new role in a DSI context may have longer‐term benefits to quality of life and social support for both the older person with DSI and their carer, that is, the dyad.

DSI defies the conventional idea of multimorbidity; instead, two disabilities combine to create a qualitatively different and more complex problem, and one that is as much ‘social’ as health. In this study, carers' understandings of DSI were juxtaposed against their encounters with siloed health care professionals and a system that treats DSI as the intersection of two distinct conditions, each with their own professional practice and service delivery. In the absence of broader systemic recognition of DSI, the adoption of a conscious caring approach will enable carers to better understand their role as advocates for their family members and understand the social aspects of caring.

In parallel, improving health and social support pivots on better health professionals' understanding of the combined impacts of DSI. However, not only do health professionals feel underprepared for the complexity of DSI, but time constraints and the need to adopt a range of other ‘roles’ (such as counsellor, navigator, trainer) limit capacity to respond appropriately to need (Fraser et al. 2019). These are missed opportunities. Additionally, health professionals, including registered nurses (RN) and GPs, lack specific education and support in developing complex communication skills, fundamental to improving quality of care, patient safety and communication. Carers then become the default communication pathway, the ‘eyes and ears’, but with limited recognition of the role they play when seeking support in health and social care. Carers can, with the right supports in place, ‘bridge this social gap’ by connecting to formal and informal health and social networks through a process described in this study as conscious caring; however, without a better societal understanding of DSI, including by healthcare professionals, carers operate in isolation. Broadly, we argue that recognition of DSI as a separate disability could address barriers to effective communication and improve integration of care between service providers (including formal and informal care support staff) and those with DSI. Developing support systems and approaches, such as conscious caring, that recognise, promote and champion the carer role in this context has significant potential for improving quality of life, social engagement and interpersonal relations for their family member.

sec.title: Strengths
sec.p: This qualitative study recommends a ‘conscious caring’ approach for optimising support for older persons with DSI and their family carers in Australia. This approach has the potential to support the dyad through investment in social relational aspects of DSI and to reduce stress as carers transition and adjust to their new caring role. Integrating this dyadic approach more broadly has the capacity to improve health care experiences, social engagement and quality of life for their partner or parent with DSI.

sec.title: Limitations
sec.p: This study interviewed carers at one point in time. It is recognised that adaptation to a new role takes time, and further adaptation to the caring role in a DSI context may have occurred for the participants in this study. Future studies would benefit from a longitudinal perspective to accurately map key transition points and the relevant supports that facilitated change over time. In addition, it is recognised that this study lacks gender and cultural diversity in carer participants.

sec.title: Recommendations for Further Research
sec.p: Future studies could include the experiences of primary care health professionals exploring barriers to effective communication and potential strategies to meet the educational needs of primary health care professionals. This study focused on carer experiences, but a strong narrative throughout reflects dissatisfaction with health care interactions (particularly hospital experiences); to uphold key Australian standards of care (Australian Government 2021), such as communicating for safety and partnering with consumer standards, there is an urgent need to integrate lived experiences with pragmatic solutions that will address cultural diversity, patient safety and improved health care experiences for those living with DSI and their families. Healthcare professionals (including registered nurses) require complex communication skills to support older adults with DSI, better integrate care, navigate systems safely and prevent adverse events. We recommend that these skills be embedded in undergraduate curriculum design and updated as professional skills in health care settings.

sec.title: Implications for Policy and Practice
sec.p: The development of a conscious caring approach may have merit in supporting carers to understand DSI, navigate key systems and effectively advocate for their family member with DSI. More broadly, DSI should be recognised in legal protections, policies and practices as a unique and distinct disability in older age, rather than two separate conditions (vision and hearing loss). DSI‐specific support services are limited and disaggregated; policy action should (1) ensure clear referral pathways to relevant services, (2) harness the power of social prescribing and (3) mandate that formal carers (through My Aged Care) have the requisite complex communication and socio‐relational skills to effectively care for those with DSI.

Above all, policy solutions need to start with the dyad (carer and person with DSI) as they are uniquely positioned to identify the specific challenges inherent in DSI. Including lived experience at every stage of the research process through co‐design processes acknowledges that older adults with DSI are best placed to offer enduring and pragmatic solutions.

sec.title: Conclusion
sec.p: The findings of this study provide a detailed account of the ‘art of caring’ in a DSI context and describe the work involved in reimagining the caring role, navigating complex and often unresponsive systems and creating social opportunities for those with DSI. We identify how approaches to care, such as ‘conscious caring’, could potentially be operationalised to benefit both the older adult with DSI and their carer or family member.
